specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between work done, force and distance moved in the direction of the force: work done = force × distance moved W = F × d
know that work done is equal to energy transferred

primer.text: Work done is the energy story behind every push and pull that actually moves something. These lessons pin down when a force counts as doing work, how the transferred joules land in different stores, and how the work done equation turns force and distance into a number you can calculate.

lessons.title: The meaning of work done
lessons.opening: Whenever a force succeeds in moving an object along the direction it acts, physicists say the force does work. That work is not lost: it is the measure of energy transferred, which is why both are counted in the same unit, the joule.
keyPoints: Work is done only when a force makes an object move through a distance along the direction of the force.
A force that fails to produce any movement transfers no energy, so no work is done.
The energy transferred when work is done equals the work done, both measured in joules.
A force acting along the direction of motion fills the object's kinetic store, while an opposing force drains energy away to the surroundings.

low.restatement: Push something and it moves: the pusher loses energy and the mover gains it, and the size of that exchange is exactly the work done. Hold something still with all your strength and nothing moves, so nothing is transferred and the work done stays at zero.
low.analogy: Treat work done as a payment for movement: the force offers the money, distance covered along the force's line earns it, and a payment with no movement is refunded — nothing changes hands.
low.examPointer: When a sketch shows a force arrow and a motion arrow, check their directions first: energy flows into the object when they agree and out of it when they oppose.

medium.restatement: Work done quantifies a mechanical transfer of energy: a force of given size acting while its point of application travels a matching distance shifts an equal quantity of energy, counted in joules, into or out of the object's stores depending on the alignment.
medium.analogy: A conveyor belt handing out energy coupons: every metre the belt drives the load forward along the push, one coupon's worth of energy changes hands.
medium.examPointer: Quote the unit joule when equating energy transferred with work done, and state the direction condition — movement along the line of the force — before claiming work has been done.

check.stem: When is work done by a force on an object?

options.text: only when the object moves along the direction of the force
options.explanation: Movement through a distance along the force's line is the defining condition.

options.text: whenever a force is applied, moving or not
options.explanation: A force with no movement transfers nothing.

options.text: only when the force is very large
options.explanation: Size does not decide whether work happens; movement does.

options.text: only when the object speeds up afterwards
options.explanation: A change of speed is not required; any movement along the force counts.

check.stem: A person applies a strong force to a heavy wall and nothing moves. How much work does the push do on the wall?

options.text: none, because the wall never moves
options.explanation: No distance is covered, so no energy is transferred by the push.

options.text: a large amount, because the push is strong
options.explanation: Force size alone transfers nothing without movement.

options.text: an amount equal to the pusher's tiredness
options.explanation: Muscle effort is not the measure of mechanical work here.

options.text: a small non-zero amount
options.explanation: With zero movement the work done on the wall is exactly zero.

check.stem: A rope pulls a sledge forward, along its direction of travel. What happens to the sledge's stores?

options.text: its kinetic store fills as energy is transferred to it
options.explanation: A force acting along the motion fills the mover's kinetic store.

options.text: its gravitational store empties as it is pulled
options.explanation: Nothing about the pull changes height.

options.text: its thermal store fills immediately and only
options.explanation: Heating of surroundings belongs to opposing forces, not the forward pull.

options.text: its stores stay exactly as they were
options.explanation: Work done along the motion always transfers energy in.

check.stem: A frictional force drags backwards on a moving cart, opposite to its motion. What does that force do?

options.text: it removes energy from the cart, transferring it to the surroundings
options.explanation: An opposing force drains the mover's store and dissipates energy by heating.

options.text: it does no work because it opposes the motion
options.explanation: Opposing forces do work too — negative-direction work on the stores.

options.text: it adds energy to the cart's kinetic store
options.explanation: That is what an aligned force does, not an opposing one.

options.text: it only changes the cart's direction of travel
options.explanation: The cart keeps its heading; energy is what changes hands.

check.stem: Which unit counts both the work done by a force and the energy it transfers?

options.text: the joule
options.explanation: Work done and energy transferred share the joule.

options.text: the newton
options.explanation: Newtons measure force, not the transfer.

options.text: the watt
options.explanation: Watts measure power — energy transferred per second.

options.text: the kilogram
options.explanation: Kilograms measure mass.

check.stem: State the condition under which a force does work on an object.
check.modelAnswer: The object must move through a distance along the direction of the applied force; without that movement, no work is done.

check.stem: State the relationship between the energy transferred when work is done and the size of that work.
check.modelAnswer: The energy transferred is equal to the work done, and both quantities are measured in joules.

check.stem: Explain why leaning against a closed door and pushing hard does no work on the door, even though your muscles tire.
check.modelAnswer: Work requires the point of application of the force to travel some distance. The door stays closed and nothing moves, so no distance is covered, no energy is transferred by the push, and the work done on the door is zero — the tiredness comes from muscle chemistry, not from mechanical work.

check.stem: A sledge is hauled 4 m forward along flat ground, then dragged 4 m back along the same path by an identical backward-acting frictional pull. Describe the work each force does.
check.modelAnswer: The forward haul does work on the sledge and fills its kinetic store along the first leg, while the frictional drag acts opposite to the return motion, removing energy from the sledge and dissipating it to the thermal stores of the surroundings by heating.

lessons.title: Work done in everyday examples
lessons.opening: Three everyday scenes make the idea concrete: pushing a box across a floor, lifting a ball upward, and a bird battling through the air. In each one a force acts over a distance, and the energy movements between stores can be traced store by store.
keyPoints: Pushing a box across the floor transfers energy from the person to the box while the force moves it along.
Lifting a ball transfers energy mechanically into its gravitational potential store as it gains height.
A bird flying forwards does work against air resistance, draining its kinetic store into thermal stores of the bird and the air.
Whether energy lands in a useful store or is dissipated depends on which direction the force acts relative to the movement.

low.restatement: Push a box and your effort lands in its motion and in the warming floor; lift a ball and your effort lands in its height; fly as a bird and your effort leaks into the air as heat. Same law, three destinations.
low.analogy: Three delivery vans leaving one depot: the address — aligned push, upward lift, headwind drag — decides which warehouse, motion or height or warmth, receives the parcel of energy.
low.examPointer: Name the force, the distance and the receiving store in every description: that trio earns the marks in examples like these.

medium.restatement: In each scene the work done by the named force equals the energy it transfers, but the destination store differs: aligned pushes feed kinetic stores, lifts feed gravitational stores, and drags against motion dissipate energy to thermal stores of object and surroundings alike.
medium.analogy: A pay slip routed three ways: the same wage (work done) lands in a current account (kinetic), a savings account (gravitational) or is spent at once (dissipated heat), depending on the route chosen.
medium.examPointer: When asked about a specific example, tie the direction of the force to the store that fills or empties — opposing forces always route energy to thermal stores.

check.stem: A person slides a box forward along the floor. Where does the energy transferred by the pushing force end up?

options.text: in the box's motion and in warming the box and floor
options.explanation: The aligned push fills the kinetic store; friction's opposing work warms the surfaces.

options.text: back inside the person's muscles, untouched
options.explanation: Energy leaves the person; it does not return by itself.

options.text: nowhere, because sliding costs nothing
options.explanation: Movement against any resistance always involves transfers.

options.text: entirely in the box's gravitational store
options.explanation: Height does not change on a level floor.

check.stem: A ball is lifted steadily upward. Which transfer does the lifting force perform?

options.text: a mechanical transfer into the ball's gravitational potential store
options.explanation: Lifting against gravity fills the gravitational store as height grows.

options.text: a heating transfer into the ball's thermal store
options.explanation: Steady lifting is not primarily a heating process.

options.text: an electrical transfer along the lifter's arm
options.explanation: The transfer route here is mechanical, not electrical.

options.text: no transfer, because the speed stays constant
options.explanation: Constant speed does not mean no transfer; height is changing.

check.stem: A bird flies level at constant speed through still air. Which statement about its work is right?

options.text: it does work against air resistance, and that energy is dissipated to thermal stores
options.explanation: The bird pushes forward against drag, so energy drains from its kinetic store into warmth.

options.text: it does no work because its speed is constant
options.explanation: Level flight still requires working against drag every second.

options.text: all its transferred energy goes to its gravitational store
options.explanation: Level flight changes no height.

options.text: the energy it spends returns to its kinetic store untouched
options.explanation: Drag constantly drains the store; the bird must keep refilling it.

check.stem: In the lifted-ball example, which statement about the stores is correct?

options.text: energy leaves the lifter and fills the ball's gravitational store
options.explanation: The lifting force does work and the height store fills.

options.text: energy multiplies as it passes between stores
options.explanation: Conservation forbids multiplication; amounts are transferred.

options.text: the ball's kinetic store grows while height increases at steady speed
options.explanation: Steady speed keeps the kinetic store level.

options.text: the surroundings gain nothing at all
options.explanation: Small heating effects are always present in real lifting.

check.stem: Which everyday case involves a force doing work that immediately dissipates energy to the surroundings?

options.text: a bird pushing through air resistance
options.explanation: Drag work ends as heating of the bird and the air.

options.text: a box resting untouched on the ground
options.explanation: No movement, no work.

options.text: a ball held motionless in an open hand
options.explanation: Holding still transfers no mechanical energy.

options.text: a satellite coasting far from any atmosphere
options.explanation: With no resistive force to work against, nothing dissipates.

check.stem: Name the store that fills when a ball is lifted to a height.
check.modelAnswer: The ball's gravitational potential store fills as it is lifted higher in the gravitational field.

check.stem: State which force a flying bird works against in level flight.
check.modelAnswer: The bird does work against air resistance, also called drag, as it moves forward.

check.stem: Explain why pushing a box along a rough floor warms the box and the floor slightly.
check.modelAnswer: The pushing force does work as the box moves, and the rough surface drags against the motion. That opposing force also does work, taking energy from the box and dissipating it by heating to the thermal stores of the box and the floor.

check.stem: A crane lifts a steel beam upward at constant speed. Compare the work done by the cable's pull with the work done by gravity on the beam.
check.modelAnswer: The cable's upward pull does work along the lift and fills the beam's gravitational potential store, while gravity acts downward opposite the movement, doing work that drains that store — at constant speed the two effects balance, so the beam's kinetic store stays level.

lessons.title: Calculating work done
lessons.opening: The work done equation turns the idea into numbers: multiply the force by the distance travelled along that force and you have the energy transferred in joules. A formula triangle keeps the three quantities straight when rearranging.
keyPoints: Work done = force × distance travelled along the force's line, written W = F × d.
Force enters the equation in newtons and distance in metres, giving work done in joules or newton-metres.
A formula triangle covering W with F and d on show reproduces every rearrangement of the equation.
Only the distance component along the force's own line counts toward the work done by that force.

low.restatement: Pick the force, measure how far the thing moved along that push, and multiply: the answer is the energy handed over. The triangle is the pocket version — hide the quantity you want and the layout of the other two shows the operation.
low.analogy: A vending machine: insert force, insert distance along the slot, and the machine dispenses the exact number of joules — wrong slot alignment, wrong payout.
low.examPointer: Convert to newtons and metres before multiplying so the answer lands in joules, and quote the unit with the number.

medium.restatement: W = F × d prices a transfer in joules: F in newtons, d in metres measured along the force's line. The triangle encodes the three rearrangements — W = Fd, F = W/d, d = W/F — for the quantity an exam question hides.
medium.analogy: Three cogs labelled W, F and d in a row: cover any one and the remaining two show whether to multiply or divide.
medium.examPointer: For angled pulls, use the distance along the force's direction, not the full path length, and say so in your working.

check.stem: Which product gives the work done by a steady force?

options.text: force × distance moved along the force
options.explanation: That product is exactly the energy the force transfers.

options.text: force ÷ distance moved
options.explanation: Dividing gives one rearrangement for finding force, not the definition.

options.text: force × speed
options.explanation: Speed belongs to kinetic energy, not work done.

options.text: mass × distance moved
options.explanation: Mass never appears in the work done equation.

check.stem: A force of 20 N moves an object 3 m along the force's line. How much work is done?

options.explanation: 20 × 3 = 60, so 60 J of energy is transferred.
That is 20 ÷ 3 — the wrong operation.
Adding the numbers is meaningless here.
No step of the calculation produces this value.

check.stem: Which pair of units feeds W = F × d so the answer comes out in joules?

options.text: force in newtons, distance in metres
options.explanation: Newtons times metres gives joules (equivalently newton-metres).

options.text: force in newtons, time in seconds
options.explanation: Time is not part of work done.

options.text: mass in kilograms, distance in metres
options.explanation: Mass does not enter this equation.

options.text: force in newtons, distance in centimetres
options.explanation: Centimetres must be converted to metres first.

check.stem: On the work done formula triangle, which arrangement is correct?

options.text: W on top, with F and d along the base
options.explanation: Covering W leaves F × d; covering F leaves W over d.

options.text: F on top, with W and d along the base
options.explanation: That layout would encode F = W × d, which is wrong.

options.text: d on top, with W and F along the base
options.explanation: That layout would encode d = W × F, which is wrong.

options.text: the triangle only works for speed, distance and time
options.explanation: The same triangle pattern serves many equations, including this one.

check.stem: A crate is dragged 5 m along the floor, but the rope's tension acts at a slack angle so the crate's motion is only partly along the pull. What best describes the work done by the tension?

options.text: only the distance component along the pull counts toward the work done
options.explanation: The equation uses distance travelled in the force's own direction.

options.text: the full 5 m counts regardless of the angle
options.explanation: Off-axis movement earns nothing from that force.

options.text: no work is done because of the angle
options.explanation: A partly-aligned force still does some work.

options.text: the work done doubles because of the angle
options.explanation: Angling reduces, never inflates, the along-force distance.

check.stem: State the work done equation using symbols, and name each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: W = F × d, where W is the work done, F is the applied force and d is the distance the object travels along the force's line of action.

check.stem: State the unit of work done and one equivalent combined unit.
check.modelAnswer: Work done is measured in joules, which is equivalent to the newton-metre.

check.stem: Explain why the distance must lie along the direction of the force for W = F × d to give the work done by that force.
check.modelAnswer: The equation counts only the energy transfer caused by that particular force. Movement perpendicular to the force involves no push or drag along its line, so only distance travelled in the force's own direction represents energy moved by it.

check.stem: The brakes of a van apply a force of 400 N and bring it to a stop over 30 m. Calculate the work done by the brakes.
check.modelAnswer: W = F × d = 400 × 30 = 12 000 J, so the brakes transfer 12 000 J of energy while stopping the van.

glossary.definition: The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance along the direction of the force.
The unit of energy and of work done; one joule equals one newton-metre.
Spread to the surroundings, usually by heating, so the energy is no longer held in a useful store.

workedExample.prompt: A car moving at speed begins to apply the brakes. The brakes of the car apply a force of 500 N which brings it to a stop after 23 m. Calculate the work done by the brakes in stopping the car.
steps: List the known quantities: force F = 500 N and distance d = 23 m.
State the equation: W = F × d.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The brakes do 11 500 J of work in stopping the car.
